newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: INTERVIEW-Mobil plans to spend $60 mln in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Mobil plans to spend $60 mln in Pakistan.

text.p: Mobil Corp said on Wednesday it planned to invest $60 million in lubricant oil and liquid petroleum gas (LPG) storage, blending, distribution and marketing operations in Pakistan.

Mark Green, chief executive and president of Mobil Oil Pakistan (Private) Ltd, a 100 percent Mobil Corp subsidiary, told Reuters that Mobil Corp had committed an initial investment of $10 million in production and marketing of lubricant oils.
The remaining $50 million would be invested in the next three to five years in the LPG project, he said.

Both the lubricant business and the LPG project would be run as separate joint venture companies of Mobil Corp and Pakistan's Army Welfare Trust (AWT), one of the biggest conglomerates run by the Fauji (army) Foundation.

Green said that with Pakistan's demand for petroleum products projected to grow at nine to 10 percent a year, Mobil would remain a serious bidder for future oil and gas exploration, production, marketing and refining opportunities.
"In fact a Mobil team is here now looking at exploration and production projects...and we are really interested in finding a big gas field," he said.
"The reason we are in Pakistan is that Mobil had a renewed focus on South Asia," Green said.

He said Mobil started looking at Pakistan, Bangladesh and India for joint ventures after it invested more than $1 billion dollars in Kazakhstan a few years ago in oil and gas exploration and production.
Central Asian fuel resources could not have a better route to the world than through Pakistan, Green added.
He said Mobil had studied opportunities for developing a port in Somniani, near Karachi. "It is still up for consideration and we will continue to look at it."
Green said the proposed oil pipeline from Turkmenistan to Pakistan could spark a lot of interest and investment in the region.

The U.S. Unocal Corp and Saudi-based Delta Oil Company have planned a 1,800-km (1,120-mile) oil pipeline from Chardzhou in Turkmenistan to Pakistan's Gawadar port, but the project has been held up as the route runs through Afghanistan.

Green said Mobil, with its Pakistani partner AWT, was in the process of upgrading to international standards a recently acquired lubricant oil blending plant in the industrial estate of Hub, near Karachi.

He said Mobil would have a 70 percent stake in the lubricant business joint venture -- Mobil Askari Lubricants Ltd -- and was likely to take 10 to 20 percent of the estimated 300,000 tonnes a year lubricant market within the next three to five years.

He said the plant would have an annual production capacity of 25,000 to 30,000 tonnes on a single shift basis and would produce the full line of Mobil lubricants for both transport and industrial applications. But top-tier synthetic lubricants would be imported from Mobil's plant in France.

He said Mobil and AWT had submitted a joint bid for constructing LPG storage and distribution facilities at Karachi's Port Qasim, and planned to build LPG depots throughout the country for efficient marketing of the product.
He said Pakistan was producing about 200,000 tonnes of LPG a year but the projected demand was likely to soar up to a million tonnes by the year 2005.
